1.text:
Move the colors of this text clearly further apart.

- Make the lighter color lighter, or the darker color darker.
- Locked to a brand color? Put a solid, contrasting shape behind the text, in the same frame.
- Much larger text needs less contrast.

2.text: Text this faint can be hard to read for some people, and not only people with low vision. Glare, a dim screen, or tired eyes can make it harder for anyone. Right now this text measures {measured}, and it needs {required}. Closing that gap does not mean giving up your color. One option is to darken the text slightly. Another is to change the surface behind it, or to keep this color for larger or bolder words. Which way fits the design is your call.

3.text: Contrast is a measure of how different two colors are in lightness. The more different they are, the easier the words are to pick out, and a bar is set so that ordinary text stays readable for as many people as possible. Right now this text measures {measured}, and it needs {required}. The gap is a constraint, and there is more than one way through it. You could darken the same color a little. You could take a color that already passes from elsewhere in your file. You could keep the color but use it for larger or bolder text, where the bar is lower. You could put it on a darker surface. Or you could keep it as an accent and set the words themselves in a darker shade. Each of these keeps your intent, so you choose the one that suits the design.

button text:medium:normal:2.text: Button text that falls short of the {required} contrast (currently {measured}) can be hard to tap when users are struggling to see it. This matters especially for people with slightly older eyes or when they are reading on a phone in bright sunlight, because low contrast reduces legibility and slows down interaction. You could try increasing the text contrast or using a darker shade for the button label to keep it readable in those conditions.

button text:medium:normal:3.text: The contrast rule exists to keep text readable for everyone, so the bar is set at {required} to ensure enough difference between text and background. Your button text currently measures {measured}, which falls short of that target. One option is to keep the same hue but darken it a bit, or pick a passing colour already in your palette that meets the ratio. You could also change the button’s fill colour so the gap between text and fill widens. Buttons are things people must find and press, so being easy to read matters more here. This helps users with tired eyes or older vision read the button easily.

caption:high:normal:2.text: The caption may be hard to read for people with slightly older eyes, especially when reading on a phone in bright sunlight. Because the contrast is only {measured} while the standard calls for {required}, the text can blend into the background and cause strain. Small text like captions is the hardest to read when contrast is low. You could improve readability by choosing a noticeably darker shade for the caption colour.

caption:high:normal:3.text: The contrast of your caption is {measured}, below the needed {required}, so it may be hard to read. The idea behind the rule is that enough difference in lightness lets the eye separate text from its background, which is why a minimum ratio is set. Small text needs a bigger difference because thin, small letters are harder to pick out. You could keep the same hue and darken it quite a bit, or pick a darker shade that already exists in your palette for the caption. This matters most when reading on a phone in bright sunlight, where low contrast fades quickly.

decorative:high:large:2.text: Because this text is decorative, it isn’t required to meet a contrast minimum, but if it does carry information it could become hard to read, especially for eyes that are a little older. The current contrast is {measured} while the standard asks for {required}. If the words matter, use a darker shade for them, and keep the lighter colour only for pure decoration.

decorative:high:large:3.text: Because decorative text isn’t required to meet a contrast minimum, the current {measured} ratio and the {required} ratio don’t pose a formal problem as long as the words carry no information. The idea behind contrast is that it measures how light the text is compared with its background, on a scale from 1:1 to 21:1, to ensure readability when needed. If the lettering does convey meaning, you could keep the colour by darkening it a little, swapping to a passing colour already in the palette, using it for larger or bolder text, placing it on a darker surface, or treating it as an accent while rendering the main words in a darker shade. This lets the design stay vibrant without sacrificing legibility.

heading:low:large:2.text: A heading that falls short of the needed contrast can be hard to read for people with slightly older eyes, especially when they are reading on a phone in bright sunlight. The current contrast is {measured} but should be at least {required}. Large text needs less contrast than small text, so you are close. A slightly darker text colour should be enough to get there.

heading:low:large:3.text: The contrast of your heading is {measured}, which is below the {required} level. This matters because a minimum difference between text and background keeps text legible for everyone, and large text only needs a lower bar than small text. Your heading is close, so a small change should be enough. You could keep the same hue and darken it a little, or choose a passing colour that is already in your palette. Another option is to change the surface behind the heading so the difference grows. This respects the idea behind the rule, which is clear communication, while keeping your design intent.

unknown:high:large:2.text: When large text doesn’t meet the contrast needed ({measured} vs {required}), it can strain readers, especially older eyes or when reading on a phone in bright sunlight. Low contrast makes letters blend into the background, so people may miss important information or have to squint. One option is to boost the contrast by darkening the text colour quite a bit, keeping the visual style while improving readability.

unknown:high:large:3.text: The contrast between your text and its background is {measured}, but it needs to be at least {required}. That is too low, which can make reading difficult for people with older eyes or tired eyes after a long day. The idea behind the contrast rule is that a clear difference in lightness keeps text legible for everyone, and the bar is set to protect readability across conditions. You could keep the same hue but darken it quite a bit, or choose a passing colour already in your palette. Using the colour for larger text, or changing the surface behind it, are also good options.
